The landing list

Sixty-eight claims are on this page. Eleven of them were unresolved on 10 September, and every one sits in finances by buyer, costings, the production facility or the ask. Nothing else blocks the application. Seven closed on 11 September, when Xero came back and the invoices, the carrier bills, the register and the live sheet were read line by line. Q6 and Q7 were rewritten the same evening against the siting ruling, so no answer is held any more. Four are left. Two new threads opened and both are smaller than what they replaced: a batch of 15 beds no invoice accounts for, and a shared buyer table whose key is broken in 4,551 places.

The Butterfly board minutes Kristy Bloomfield's related-party declaration, which is the only thing standing between Q8 and the record. The same day Nic asks Sam at Defy what a second press costs, which is the first real number under the plant allowance and the only thing that can size the Sefa approach. One day closes or informs four of the eleven.

Closed 11 SepRuling 7
We do not have a demand number, and we should stop implying one

Every bed figure on the record is somebody's impression of a population nobody has counted. Adding them makes 778, which puts a figure scoped to one Elder's wallet alongside one scoped to the children of an outstation and one with no scope written down at all. It is not a quantity of anything and it cannot survive a second question.

So present the acts instead. An act is a thing somebody did. Money moved. A council wrote. An Elder said she would pay for them herself. Those are checkable by anyone, and they are the only part of the demand record that is evidence.

How to say it

Lead with what was paid. Four organisations, 320 beds, $273,966 settled. It is the only rung nobody can push back on, and it proves the price at the same time.
Name the organisation and let the number follow it. "Palm Island Community Company asked" is evidence. "Palm Island needs 40 beds" is an impression wearing a number.
When a number is used, it stays attached to the act that produced it and to what it covers. A figure with no scope is printed with its scope missing.
Never state a demand total. If asked for one, say we do not have a demand measure, say why, and offer the household count instead.
Two organisations in Maningrida have bought from us and one of them asked for more. Repeat buyers in one place say more about demand than any count.
The largest number on the record came up once in a meeting and is the weakest thing we hold.

How many a community takes, from the ones we know

Two earlier attempts to size this failed. Beds cannot be derived from Census overcrowding, because that standard counts bedrooms and we supply beds. And no rate hides under the recorded asks, because each is scoped to a different population. This works because it uses a different input: what communities actually took once beds were available.

Utopia is dispersed homelands and not a town, and it is where we have gone deepest. At four times the density of anywhere else it sizes nothing but itself.

A plant's first year is the size of a town's first phase

A new plant makes about 200 beds in its first year. A town of 2,500 people sits between 122 and 204 beds on this range. So one plant, running a year, covers roughly what a community that size has been observed to take. Nobody designed that to line up, which is what makes it a check on both models.

Three things to say every time the number is used. It is bounded by what we could afford to make, so it describes our funding as much as their need. It is a floor, because all three have asked for more. And the plainest claim needs no model at all: beds have gone to eleven communities and not one has come back to say it has enough.

When a funder asks what the demand is

They are asking whether anyone will take these beds. The answer is that four organisations have already paid for 320, including a research centre that paid for a hundred up front before one was made, and a schools operator in Maningrida that bought the first full run off our own press. Five more communities have asked and we can name who asked in every case.

What we cannot give them is a number for how many beds are needed, and we say so. One community counting properly would change that: four questions per household, done by a local person paid for the work. Nobody has done it yet.

Twelve rulings

Given by Ben in an interview on 11 September 2026, fourteen days before QBE closes. Each one settles something that was blocking a slide, an answer or the sheet. They are the reason Q6 and Q7 are now held, and the reason the demand tally came off the table.

1Beds stay the counted unit, and the deck says whyThe bed is the instrument and the community enterprise is the outcome. Chosen over leading with enterprises because 320 beds are paid for and no enterprise is trading yet.
2Plants are sited on relationship and readinessPalm Island goes first on asked-for, a local operator and 131 beds already delivered. Q6's 200-beds-a-year test is dropped and Q7's largest-demand claim is false and comes out.
3The four locked problem modules open the deckReplacing slide 3's four national statistics. Every figure guarded in code with a source URL and a grade.
4Need is shown as the household measureOvercrowding, which AIHW names as the risk factor in the Strep A chain. Arnhem Land 70%, Central Australia 49%, against 15% nationally. The demand tally is rejected outright.
5What the $300,000 changes is that a measured cost existsNobody lends against a community-made bed because nobody knows what one costs to make in a community. Two plants produce that number in year one.
6Snow concentration is said plainly as the riskOne funder was more than half the year and there is no ask to replace it. Needs the A Curious Tractor ledger connected before a number can be defended.
7The four 100-bed pools go where beds already wentTennant Creek, Utopia, Palm Island, Maningrida. Each has deployed beds, a relationship and cleared voices.
8The strongest voice is Dianne Stokes on the washing machine“Every time I go away, it’s like it’s calling me. Come back home.” On Pakkimjalki Kari, which she named in Warumungu.
9The one chart to add is the two kinds of money that never meetCatalytic capital pays Goods for first stock. Buyers pay the community enterprise and that money never reaches Goods.
10The sheet's two urgent surfacesThe production log with run days, which turns 48 beds a month from a ruling into a rate. And community context, which has no home anywhere today.

The Commonwealth plant money, and what it changes

Ben, 11 September: the $150,000 for the Alice Springs facility is approved and ready, and a second $150,000 for a Goods facility on the same route is highly likely. A plant costs $150,000 and a plant grant brings $150,000, so this money does something unusual to the arithmetic.

ScenarioPlantsThe year needsFundedGap
The raise as it stands2$747,950$600,000$147,950
Alice Springs counted in, as a third site3$897,950$750,000$147,950
Both land, both on new sites4$1,047,950$900,000$147,950
The second facility takes one of the two QBE sites3$897,950$900,000$0
Adding plants never closes the gap. Freeing QBE money does.

In the first three rows both sides move by the same $150,000, so the year gains a plant and the hole stays exactly where it was. The gap only closes in the last row, where the Commonwealth pays for a plant QBE was already being asked to pay for, and $150,000 of the QBE request moves from plants to beds.

That last row is also the one with a disclosure in it. If the second $150,000 lands on Palm Island or Maningrida it funds an activity QBE is being asked to fund, and Q14 and Q15 have to carry it as other funding for the same purpose. If it lands on a third site it is additional capacity and the application is untouched. Ben names the site, and that one answer is worth $147,950.

The cheapest way to fund the organisation is to fund beds

Every dollar of bed money does two jobs. It pays the $276 of making and hands $474 to the organisation. So the 187 unfunded beds are $140,250 of stock and $88,638 of the running cost at the same time, which is why the bed line and the operating line cannot be added together.

It is also the only ask with a product at the end of it. A funder who will not write a cheque for accounting fees will write one for beds, and the beds pay the accounting fees.

The second press is in no ask. About $22,500, unpriced until Monday, and it decides whether the 400 beds land in June or August.

The four impact measures, and which can be evidenced today

Every ask is counted on the same four rows. Only one of them comes from a source that has been read. The others are modelled, and what replaces each is named.

MeasurePer bedGradeWhat would make it measured
A person off the floor1 bed, 1 personVerifiedNothing. It is counted from the register, one row per bed, per community. This is the only one that can be evidenced today.
Paid making2 hours, $80ModelledThe production log, with paid hours against completed beds per day. It opened this week with no entries. The $80 also assumes five beds a day; Witta runs three.
Plastic kept in use20 kg in the bed, 36 kg through the pressModelledWeighed yield per batch: input, accepted parts, offcuts and waste. Never done. 20 kg is design mass and is not measured diversion.
Money kept in the communityup to $750Verified ruleThe rule is settled and no community enterprise is trading yet, so there is no figure to report. It becomes measurable at the first community sale.
Healththe reason, never a rowNot claimedNothing, on purpose. Scabies and rheumatic heart disease are why a bed is washable and off the ground. No health study has been run and none is inferred from a delivery.
What this means for Q9 and Q10

One of four rows is countable from a source that has been read. Two are modelled and both are replaced by measurement the two plants produce in their first year, which is the same argument Q18 makes about a measured cost. The third has a settled rule and no trading enterprise behind it yet.

Saying that plainly is stronger than presenting four numbers as though they were the same kind of thing. It is also what the first fifty beds off each line are for.

Four things nobody has ruled on

Bed volumes are targets that fit inside measured capacity. No buyer has ordered year two or year three. And the running cost is held flat at $297,550 across all three years while two plants and six communities are added. Nobody has decided that; it is an assumption.

  1. Does the running cost stay at $297,550 for three years, or does it grow.
  2. Does founder pay move off $151,200 once trade carries the organisation.
  3. Who carries freight from year two. It moves break-even from 628 beds to 918.
  4. Whether year three pays for the handover, which is the only line here that is not an operating cost.

Facilitation is billed at $10,000 a community and costs about the same to deliver, so it is kept out of the income line. Counting it as income without its cost is the same mistake that produced the $937,550.

The decision turns on one price we do not have

Panels and a second press reach the same 80 beds a month. Across the 400 they cost the same when shred lands at about $3.16 a kilogram. Below that the press wins and above it the panels do, and a longer run moves the line further toward the press because the machine is bought once.

The only prices a kilogram we hold are $6.87 and $7.34. Both are for finished pressed panel, and shred should come in well under either, so the press is the likely answer. It cannot be settled until somebody reads the bag price.

Quotes QU0494 and QU0495, sent by Sam Davies on 27 August, price the 105 sheets and the 8 bulka bags. Neither is in the repo. That is the whole blocker.

01Where it stands

The applicant is The Butterfly Movement Ltd trading as Goods on Country. It asks QBE for $300,000 to build two community plants, working choices Palm Island and Maningrida, with one plant at $150,000 as the smaller case. Beds are a separate ask and are not in this request.

Three dates sit the wrong way round

QBE wants any pre-conditions met by 13 November. The Brian M. Davis board sits on 19 November and Tim Fairfax decides in late November. So the two funders who pay for beds decide after QBE needs its conditions satisfied. Q18 puts that question to QBE directly.

02The model in four answers

Four questions carry the whole thing. Every figure below is a cell in the workbook.

What is a bed worth

$750 at the factory door. $276 to make it, with $80 of paid making inside that. $474 stays with Goods on Country. Freight is charged on top at cost, its own line per community, paid by whoever buys the bed. This is a price model. The organisation is never divided by beds alone.

What is being asked for

QBE is asked for $300,000 to build two plants at $150,000 each. Beds are separate: 400 of first stock, of which Tim Fairfax covers 133 and Brian M. Davis 80, leaving 187 to find, or 54 once the $100,000 Snow ask is sent and counted as beds. Alice Springs is funded through Oonchiumpa and sits outside the raise.

What already runs

320 beds sold and paid across ten invoices, $343,481 all time. FY26 Goods receipts were $653,246. Snow was $375,000 of that, or 57%, and there is no Snow ask this year. Nothing in the plan replaces the other $275,000.

What one bed does

Two hours of paid making. 36 kg of shred through the press, 20 kg of it in the finished bed. Up to $750 kept in the community when the community sells it. One person off the floor. Health is the reason the hardware exists and is never claimed as an outcome.

04Every claim

Every number and assertion that could reach a funder, with where it comes from and how far it can be defended. Five grades. Verified means the source was read directly. Modelled means it is calculated and has not been measured. Invited means a funder asked us to apply and has not decided. Conflict means two sources disagree and a person has to rule. Unverified means one source and no second.
